quote: Subjects instructed to say the color of printed pictures and shown the picture Green often say “green” instead of “red.”
content: Error rates in the standard Stroop task are a few percent, not "often," and the sentence should be fixed. The lesson is not reversed, though. Fable's summary, "the literate subject cannot help extracting the meaning," is the essay's point. Reading intrudes automatically, and the literate reader of the arguer's paper takes in "box B contains the diamond" whether they want to or not. That is why "it helps to be illiterate." The Stroop subject who reports the colour correctly does so by working against an automatic reading, several hundred milliseconds of interference, and the essay asks readers to do the same work with the bottom line: see the ink as a physical trace of a bidding process, against the automatic meaning of the words.

quote: So the handwriting of the curious inquirer is entangled with the signs and portents and the contents of the boxes, whereas the handwriting of the clever arguer is evidence only of which owner paid the higher bid.
content: The quoted sentence is about "the handwriting," the bottom line. What the listed facts are worth to a listener who knows the selection process is the subject of the next essay, What Evidence Filtered Evidence?, and the sequence divides the topics that way on purpose. The genetic-fallacy charge is answered in the essay's closing paragraph: "This is intended as a caution for your own thinking, not a Fully General Counterargument against conclusions you don't like... The world's cleverest arguer may point out that the Sun is shining, and yet it is still probably daytime." Fable grants that the lesson about one's own reasoning is sound and supported by Kunda. That lesson is the essay's stated scope.

quote: It may help to visualize a collection of worlds—Everett branches or Tegmark duplicates—within which there is some objective frequency at which box A or box B contains a diamond.
content: What the scaffolding does is make counterfactual dependence visible: "in worlds with different portents, a different probability is written at the bottom." Possible-worlds semantics is the standard analysis of counterfactual dependence in philosophy, independent of any physics, and the essay offers the physics only as "It may help to visualize." A Bayesian is also allowed to use physical chances where they exist. The Principal Principle connects credence to known chance without making probability a frequency (Lewis 1980, "A Subjectivist's Guide to Objective Chance," no DOI). The Everett and Tegmark names are there for vividness. The substance is that the curious inquirer's ink varies across possible worlds with the evidence and the arguer's ink does not.
